beats.narration_text: Claude Opus is smartest but costs five times more. Haiku is cheap. You have no idea which one makes sense for your task. This is Liam, in for Bear.

props.segment: The Pareto Frontier: Finding the Cheapest Model That Solves Your Task
props.command: I need to pick between Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku for my task. Opus is 5× more expensive but smarter. Which one sits on the pareto frontier for my use case?

beats.narration_text: The question: how do you know which model to use for a task — without trying them all and paying for them all?

props.title: Which model — without paying for all three?
props.body: Pick per task — without running every model.

beats.narration_text: Run the same eval suite against multiple models. Plot quality — accuracy percentage — against cost in dollars. The pareto frontier is the curve of non-dominated points. A point is on the frontier if you cannot improve accuracy without paying more, or paying more without improving accuracy. Your task's optimal model sits on that frontier — not at the top of the accuracy axis, not at the bottom of the cost axis. On the frontier.

props.title: Non-dominated points
props.body: No accuracy gained without more cost. No cost cut without loss.

beats.narration_text: Here is the scatter plot. Customer-support classification task. X axis: cost per call. Y axis: accuracy. Three dots. Opus: 98% accuracy at eight cents per call. Haiku: 82% accuracy at one cent per call. Sonnet: 90% accuracy at four cents per call. Draw the frontier. It passes through Sonnet. Opus is above the frontier — you can get 90% for half the price. Haiku is below — you lose 8 points of accuracy to save three cents. Sonnet is the rational choice. 90% is good enough for this task. You save four cents per call. Across 100,000 calls: four thousand dollars back in your budget.

The accumulation is how you find the frontier. Run the same eval across all models. Record accuracy, cost, and latency per cell. Plot. The frontier draws itself. The model that wins is not always obvious before the sweep — Sonnet was not obviously the right answer. The sweep proved it.

props.title: The sweep finds the frontier
props.body: One eval, all models. Plot cost vs quality.

beats.narration_text: The sweep in practice is five steps, left to right. One: build your eval suite — ten representative tasks that reflect real usage. Two: run all three models against the same suite. Three: collect the quality and cost pair for each model. Four: plot the scatter. This is where the decision happens — the data takes a shape, and the frontier becomes visible. Five: pick the frontier model for your quality threshold. Each step has a code equivalent: the loop is three lines, the plot is one function call. The sweep is not an expensive research project. It is a script you run once before you commit to a model — and run again whenever pricing or quality shifts.

The pareto method: sweep all three models, find the frontier, pick the cost-quality optimum. For this task, Sonnet at 90% and four cents a call beats Opus by four thousand dollars per hundred thousand calls. Run the sweep. The frontier shows you what intuition cannot.

artifactLines: Run the same eval suite across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku. Plot accuracy against cost.
The pareto frontier passes through Sonnet: 90% accuracy at $0.04 per call — not $0.08.
$4,000 back per 100,000 calls: the frontier catches what intuition misses.
The optimal model sits on the frontier — not at the accuracy ceiling, not at the price floor.
